opus-5.5.text:
I'd say the biggest change isn't one single number going up. It's that the *way* the model learns a new task has qualitatively shifted.

With 1.0, every new task felt like a small project of its own. If we wanted the robot to fold a towel, or pick items from a cluttered bin, we had to collect a fairly large amount of task-specific demonstration data, tune things, and even then it was brittle. Change the lighting, move the table a little, swap in an object it hadn't seen, and performance dropped quickly. So 1.0 was really learning tasks one by one, and the knowledge didn't transfer that well between them.

With 2.0, the core idea was to move from learning individual skills to learning a more general understanding of the physical world, and then letting tasks sit on top of that. We scaled up and diversified the pretraining data a lot: different scenes, different embodiments, a lot more video of how objects move and how people interact with them. We also put more effort into the world-model side, so the model has some sense of what will happen if it takes an action, rather than just mapping images to motor commands.

The practical result is a few things. First, data efficiency. For a new task we now need far fewer demonstrations to get to a usable success rate, because the model already "knows" a lot about grasping, contact, and object dynamics. Second, generalization. When we test in environments it hasn't seen, with new objects and new layouts, the drop-off is much smaller than before. Third, long-horizon tasks. 1.0 was mostly good at short atomic actions. 2.0 can chain steps together more reliably and recover when something goes slightly wrong midway, which matters a lot in the real world.

That said, I want to be honest. We're still far from a robot that can walk into any home and just do things. Dexterous manipulation, deformable objects, and really long, open-ended tasks are still hard. Success rates that look good in a lab aren't the same as reliability you can deploy. So I'd describe 2.0 as crossing from "it can do the tasks we trained it on" to "it's starting to learn new tasks the way a foundation model should." To me that shift in learning paradigm matters more than any individual benchmark.

r001.rationale: It contrasts 1.0 learning tasks one by one with 2.0 learning a general physical-world model that supports tasks on top, communicating a shift toward one model serving multiple tasks.

r002.rationale: It says 2.0 needs far fewer demonstrations, but does not state the reduction from roughly 100 examples to roughly 20.

fable-5.1.text:
The biggest difference is in how much data it takes for the model to pick up a new task. With 1.0, if you wanted the robot to do something it hadn't seen before, say folding a towel in a new kitchen or sorting objects on a different table, you basically had to collect a fresh batch of demonstrations and fine-tune on them. It worked, but it was expensive, and every new task felt like starting over. The model didn't carry much over from what it had already learned.

With 2.0 the model has a much stronger prior. We trained it on a far larger and more diverse mix of embodied data, plus a lot of video and language, so it comes in with a reasonable understanding of what objects are, how they move, and what a task description is asking for. In practice that means for many tasks we see something like an order of magnitude drop in demonstrations needed to reach the same success rate. Some simple tasks it can attempt zero-shot from a language instruction, which 1.0 simply couldn't do.

The second thing I'd point to is generalization. In 1.0, success was tightly bound to the exact setup it was trained in. Change the lighting, swap the object for one of a different color, move the camera a bit, and performance would fall apart. 2.0 is noticeably more robust to those variations. It's still not where we want it to be, but the gap between "works in the lab" and "works in a new environment" has narrowed a lot.

I'd be honest that there's still a long way to go. Long-horizon tasks, anything that needs fine manipulation or recovery from mistakes, those are still hard. And the data-efficiency gains are uneven across task types. But if I had to summarize it, 1.0 was a system you had to teach every task; 2.0 is a system that has learned how to learn tasks, and that's a qualitative shift rather than just a number going up.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between getting better at a task you’ve already trained on and getting better at learning a new task. To compare 2.0 with 1.0, I’d look at how much demonstration data each needs, how quickly it reaches reliable performance, and whether it can apply what it has learned when the objects or environment change. Without specific results in front of us, I wouldn’t put a number on the improvement. The meaningful test is whether 2.0 can learn unfamiliar tasks with less guidance and perform them consistently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how to compare task learning, but does not say that 1.0 trained a separate downstream model per task or that 2.0 uses one model for multiple tasks.

sol-6.1.text: I’d assess it by how much experience the robot needs to learn a task, how reliably it performs afterward, and whether it can apply what it learned to a new situation. To compare 2.0 with 1.0 fairly, we’d need to test them on the same tasks under the same conditions. Without those results, I wouldn’t put a number on the improvement. The meaningful advance would be learning with fewer demonstrations and needing less retraining when the objects or environment change.
